planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or fall onto a firm, weed-free seedbed, pressing seed lightly into the soil surface rather than burying it deeply.

directions: Direct sow in early spring or late fall onto a firm, weed-free seedbed, pressing seed lightly into the surface since it needs light to germinate. Choose a well-drained, low-fertility site in full sun; established plants tolerate drought and poor soils and resent heavy clay or overly rich beds. This compact, cool-season bunchgrass forms a fine-textured tuft of blue-green foliage topped by narrow, spike-like flower panicles in late spring, making it a good filler for short prairie plantings, rock gardens, and dry meadow borders. It goes semi-dormant in summer heat and looks best combined with other short natives rather than grown as a specimen.

common_name: Pheasant's Tail Grass (New Zealand Wind Grass)

planting.note: Set out nursery divisions or transplants in spring after frost danger passes, spacing plants to allow the arching foliage room to display its fountain shape.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring in well-drained soil, choosing a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in hotter climates to keep the foliage color from bleaching. It tolerates light, infrequent irrigation once established but performs best with even moisture and does not like winter wet combined with heavy clay. The narrow, arching leaves emerge olive-green and shift to copper, bronze, and orange tones through the seasons, and airy purplish flower panicles rise above the mound in summer, giving it a soft, self-seeding presence in mixed borders and gravel gardens. In cold climates it is usually grown as an annual or protected in a container over winter.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Divide established clumps or set out nursery starts in spring, planting at the same depth they were growing and watering in well to establish the fine root system.

directions: Plant divisions or containerized starts in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic soil, siting in full sun to light shade; this South African restio tolerates both boggy soil near water features and moderate garden watering once established. It resents hard freezes and is best reserved for mild coastal or Mediterranean-climate gardens. The wiry, jointed, dark-green stems grow in dense upright clumps that resemble a rush or horsetail and bear small brown flower clusters near the stem tips in summer, giving strong vertical texture near ponds, in modern plantings, or as a textural accent among succulents and grasses.

planting.note: Divide clumps or plant nursery starts in spring directly into consistently moist to boggy soil or a shallow-water container feature.

directions: Divide an established clump or plant a nursery start in spring into consistently wet soil or a submerged pot at the edge of a pond, siting it in full sun to part shade where it will not dry out. Keep the roots saturated throughout the growing season, since this rush struggles wherever soil is allowed to dry between waterings. Its leafless, medium-green stems twist and coil into tight corkscrews, creating a distinctive sculptural accent in bog gardens, water features, and containers, and the curled stems are often cut for use in floral arrangements.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown starts in spring once the soil has warmed, giving the clump full sun and average garden soil to establish red-tinged summer color.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring in full sun and average, well-drained soil; this switchgrass selection tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic drought once its deep roots are established. Avoid heavily shaded or constantly soggy sites, which cause the upright clump to flop. Blue-green summer foliage develops wine-red tips and streaks earlier in the season than most switchgrass cultivars, deepening to burgundy and mahogany in fall, and the airy pink-tinted seed heads add movement and winter interest to borders, rain gardens, and naturalized plantings.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Set out divisions or transplants in spring into full sun and well-drained soil, allowing room for the tall clump and its billowing flower panicles.

directions: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in full sun on average to sandy soil; established clumps tolerate both drought and occasional wet spells, making this a forgiving choice for open beds and meadow-style plantings. Cut the prior season's stems back in late winter before new growth emerges. Sturdy blue-green blades stay upright through summer storms and are topped in late summer by an unusually dense, dark, cloud-like haze of tiny flowers that gives the cultivar its name, followed by tan seed heads that persist for winter interest and birds.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; deadhead spent seed heads before they mature and avoid siting near natural areas, since Miscanthus sinensis is classified as invasive in parts of the eastern and midwestern United States.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, cutting the prior year's foliage back hard in late winter before new blades emerge. A compact, dwarf sport of zebra grass, it forms a tidy rounded clump of arching blades horizontally banded in cream and green, with coppery plumes rising just above the foliage in late summer. Because this species is documented as invasive in parts of the eastern and midwestern United States, gardeners in those regions should remove flower heads before seed set, avoid planting near wild areas, and check local invasive-species guidance before adding it to the landscape.
sources: USDA Forest Service Invasive Species Database
Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring into full sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil, spacing clumps far enough apart to show off the fountain-like habit.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and moist, well-drained soil; this cultivar tolerates brief drought once established but produces the fullest flower display with regular moisture. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter to make way for fresh growth. Narrow green blades arch outward in a fountain shape and turn gold, orange, and burgundy in fall, while bottlebrush-like tan-to-copper flower spikes appear earlier in the season than on the straight species, extending the display into winter as tawny seed heads.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring or early fall in part shade to full sun, spacing closely if used as a lawn substitute or ground cover.

directions: Plant plugs or divisions in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil, choosing part shade in hot climates or full sun where summers are cooler and moisture is reliable. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes to knit together into a fine-textured groundcover and tolerates occasional mowing, making it a low-maintenance substitute for turf in small areas. The narrow, powder-blue foliage forms dense, mounding tufts a few inches tall, giving borders, pathway edges, and shady lawn alternatives a cool blue color note through the growing season.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out plugs after the soil has warmed in late spring, choosing a low spot or floodplain-type site where the deep roots can access subsurface moisture.

directions: Direct sow or plant plugs in late spring once soil has warmed, siting in full sun in a low-lying or seasonally moist spot such as a swale, arroyo edge, or floodplain; established clumps then tolerate long dry spells thanks to deep roots. Avoid deep planting of seed, since it germinates best from a shallow covering. This robust bunchgrass of the American Southwest forms one of the largest native grass clumps in the region, sending up tall, fine-textured blue-green foliage topped by large plumed seed heads in late summer, and it is valued for erosion control, wildlife habitat, and bold vertical structure in xeric and native plant gardens.

planting.note: Install plugs on close spacing in spring or fall so rhizomes can knit together into a lawn-like sward; water regularly until established, then reduce as the planting fills in.

directions: Install plugs or divisions on tight spacing in spring or fall in full sun to light shade and well-drained soil, watering consistently until the rhizomes spread and knit together into a solid patch. Once established it needs little supplemental water and can be mowed occasionally to maintain a tidy, lawn-like appearance, or left unmowed for a soft meadow look. This California native sedge spreads by rhizomes to form a fine-bladed, gray-green sward that is increasingly used as a low-water alternative to traditional turf lawns, on slopes, and in coastal and native plant gardens.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring inside a sunken barrier or root-pruning edge, since this grass spreads aggressively by rhizomes and can become a garden thug or escape into wild dune and coastal habitat if left uncontained.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and sandy, well-drained soil, and install a sunken root barrier or grow it in a large buried container, since this grass spreads quickly by aggressive rhizomes and is considered a weedy escapee in some coastal and dune habitats in the northern United States. Once established it tolerates poor, sandy, salt-exposed soil and needs little supplemental water, which is why it is traditionally used for stabilizing dunes and banks. Wide, strikingly powder-blue blades form an upright, spreading colony topped by tan wheat-like flower spikes in summer, giving strong color contrast in coastal gardens when its spread is kept in check.
